notes.title: Describing data, computed
Probability rules
notes.body: P(A and B) = P(A)·P(B|A); for independent events, P(A)·P(B). P(A or B) = P(A)+P(B)−P(A and B). Worked example: two independent deploys each fail with p=0.1. P(both fail) = 0.1×0.1 = **0.010000000000000002**. P(at least one fails) = 1 − P(neither) = 1 − 0.9² = **0.19**. Complement-first ('1 minus the boring case') solves most 'at least one' problems. Independence is an assumption to check, not a default: correlated failures break the multiplication.

notes.title: Conditional probability and Bayes
Expectation
notes.body: E[X] = Σ x·P(x): the long-run average. Worked example: a retry policy succeeds on attempt 1 with p=0.7, attempt 2 with p=0.2, attempt 3 with p=0.1 (then gives up). Expected attempts = 1×0.7 + 2×0.2 + 3×0.1 = **1.4000000000000001**. Linearity of expectation: E[X+Y] = E[X]+E[Y] even when X,Y are dependent — the workhorse for analyzing total cost, total latency, total errors across components without modeling their joint distribution.

Solving linear systems
notes.body: Worked example: 2x + y = 7 and x − y = 2. Add the equations: 3x = 9, so x = **3**; then y = 7 − 2×3 = **1**. Check: 2×3+1 = 7 ✓; 3−1 = 2 ✓. Elimination is the algorithm; the geometry is two lines intersecting at one point. A system has a unique solution exactly when the coefficient matrix is invertible (nonzero determinant).

notes.title: Determinant and invertibility
notes.body: For 2×2 [[a,b],[c,d]], det = ad − bc. Worked: A=[[1, 2], [3, 4]], det = 1×4 − 2×3 = **-2**. Nonzero → invertible → the system Ax=b has exactly one solution. det = 0 means the rows are dependent: the map crushes a dimension (area → 0). |det| is the area-scaling factor of the transformation. Singular matrices (det 0) are why 'matrix is singular' errors appear — the inverse doesn't exist.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body: - **Agent loop** — every agent is a loop around a model: perceive (observations) → reason → act (tools) → repeat. - **Tool calling** — the primitive: functions the model can invoke, with JSON schemas as the contract. - **ReAct** — Thought → Action → Observation, in a while-loop with a step budget: build this once with raw API calls. - **Loop ingredients** — a system prompt (the role), tools (the hands), memory (the notebook), and a stop condition (the discipline). - **Step budget** — the cheapest reliability feature: bounds the loop so a failing tool can't spin forever. - **Tool design** — tool design is API design: clear names, strict schemas, idempotent operations — the model is only as good as its tools. - **LangChain** — the agent-first API (`create_agent`); middleware (guardrails, retries around the loop); the integration ecosystem — breadth is why it's chosen. - **LangGraph** — agents as nodes in a graph (Pregel lineage); durable execution (the run survives interruption); checkpoints (rewind/resume first-class); human-in-the-loop as a node. - **LlamaIndex** — data-first: context augmentation as the identity; agents composed with event-driven Workflows; ingestion/indexing/retrieval first-class. - **CrewAI** — the crew metaphor (roles, goals, backstories): crews (role teams) vs flows (event orchestration); memory and guardrails per agent. - **Choose by shape** — linear tools → LangChain; branching/stateful → LangGraph; data-grounded → LlamaIndex; role teams → CrewAI. - **Semantic Kernel** — kernel + plugins, model-agnostic, C#/Python/Java. - **Agent Framework** — the documented successor path in the Microsoft landscape. - **AutoGen** — conversational multi-agent research: maintenance mode — know before adopting. - **MCP (Model Context Protocol)** — tools/resources/prompts as a standard: build once, use across harnesses. - **DSPy** — program (don't prompt) the LM: optimize prompts like weights. - **Evaluation** — trajectory scoring (did it take sensible steps?), tool-use accuracy, task success, cost/latency. - **Evaluate the trajectory** — not just the answer: a lucky success teaches nothing. - **Failure-mode field guide** — tool confusion, loop traps, context overflow, prompt injection via tool output. - **Prompt injection via tool output** — THE agent security issue: treat tool returns as untrusted input. - **Selection matrix** — score two frameworks on one task with a rubric: judgment is the deliverable.

notes.body:
Data systems fail silently and confidently. In Frontier AI Topics, these are the expensive mistakes:
- **Dirty data in, confident charts out.** No validation on ingest means every downstream number is suspect. Profile and validate before you analyze or train.
- **Train/test leakage.** Information from the future or the target leaking into features. Design the split before you touch the modeling — leakage invalidates everything after it.
- **Notebook-only work.** Analysis that can't be rerun from scratch isn't engineering. Script the pipeline; the notebook is the sketchbook, not the factory.
- **Metric myopia.** Optimizing a single metric while the business bleeds elsewhere. Every metric in Frontier AI Topics needs a counter-metric and a human-readable definition.
- **Ignoring lineage and privacy.** Not knowing where a column came from or who is allowed to see it. Document lineage; treat PII as radioactive by default.
- **One perfect run.** A pipeline that works once on your laptop is a demo. Idempotent, scheduled, monitored, alerting — that's a pipeline.

start with weak supervision/pretrained, escalate to humans for the hard cases. - **Glue/EMR prep at scale** — the data-engineering tier feeding ML training. - **SageMaker training** — managed training jobs. - **Built-in algorithms** — XGBoost, BlazingText, DeepAR: built-ins win on undifferentiated problems — custom for the novel. - **Automatic model tuning** — Bayesian hyperparameter optimization. - **Real-time endpoints** — autoscaling variants for online inference. - **Batch transform** — offline inference at scale. - **Multi-model endpoints** — many low-traffic models on one fleet: shared economics. - **Inference pipelines** — pre/post-processing chains around the model. - **Shadow deployments** — the new model scores live traffic without serving: safe validation before promotion. - **SageMaker Pipelines** — CI/CD for ML. - **Model Registry** — versioned, approved models. - **Model Monitor** — data drift and quality-decay alerts in production: the ML smoke detector. - **Lineage tracking** — which data and code produced which model. - **Data versioning** — the dataset is part of the model artifact: version it. - **Bedrock** — foundation models as API. - **Bedrock Guardrails** — the safety layer on Bedrock generation. - **Bedrock Knowledge Bases** — managed RAG: connect data sources, get retrieval-augmented generation via API — least overhead for GenAI Q&A. - **Bedrock Agents** — agentic workflows on the Bedrock substrate. - **Bedrock vs SageMaker** — API convenience vs training control: pick by differentiation. - **Exam strategy** — the specialty is scenario-dense: data prep → modeling → deployment → operations, with cost and 'least overhead' as tiebreakers. - **The exam's favorite trap** — training where inference suffices: use a pretrained model or Bedrock first.

Pitfalls & how to dodge them
notes.body:
Data systems fail silently and confidently. In AWS ML Engineering, these are the expensive mistakes:
- **Dirty data in, confident charts out.** No validation on ingest means every downstream number is suspect. Profile and validate before you analyze or train.
- **Train/test leakage.** Information from the future or the target leaking into features. Design the split before you touch the modeling — leakage invalidates everything after it.
- **Notebook-only work.** Analysis that can't be rerun from scratch isn't engineering. Script the pipeline; the notebook is the sketchbook, not the factory.
- **Metric myopia.** Optimizing a single metric while the business bleeds elsewhere. Every metric in AWS ML Engineering needs a counter-metric and a human-readable definition.
- **Ignoring lineage and privacy.** Not knowing where a column came from or who is allowed to see it. Document lineage; treat PII as radioactive by default.
- **One perfect run.** A pipeline that works once on your laptop is a demo. Idempotent, scheduled, monitored, alerting — that's a pipeline.

import math, re
from collections import Counter

DOCS = ['LangGraph checkpoints enable rewind and resume of agent runs.',
        'MCP standardizes tool exposure across agent harnesses.',
        'Q4_K_M quantization fits 70B models on consumer GPUs.']

def chunk(text, size=20, overlap=5):
    words = text.split()
    step = size - overlap
    return [' '.join(words[i:i+size]) for i in range(0, len(words), step)]

def embed(text, dim=64):
    v = Counter()
    for w in re.findall(r'\w+', text.lower()):
        v[hash(w) % dim] += 1
    return v

def cosine(a, b):
    dot = sum(a[k]*b.get(k, 0) for k in a)
    na = math.sqrt(sum(x*x for x in a.values()))
    nb = math.sqrt(sum(x*x for x in b.values()))
    return dot/(na*nb) if na and nb else 0.0

query = 'How do agents resume after interruption?'
chunks = [c for d in DOCS for c in chunk(d)]
q = embed(query)
ranked = sorted(chunks, key=lambda c: cosine(q, embed(c)), reverse=True)
top = ranked[:2]
prompt = 'Context:\n' + '\n'.join('- '+c for c in top) + f'\n\nQuestion: {query}\nAnswer:'
print(prompt)
# Lesson: retrieval quality (chunking!) dominates; the generator only answers from context.

import re

TOOLS = {
    'calculator': lambda expr: str(eval(expr, {'__builtins__': {}})),
    'search': lambda q: {'langgraph': 'checkpoints enable rewind/resume',
                         'mcp': 'standardizes tool exposure'}.get(q.lower(), 'no result'),
}

def react(question, max_steps=5):
    steps = 0
    context = ''
    while steps < max_steps:
        steps += 1
        # Thought: naive policy for the lab (a real agent asks the model)
        m = re.search(r'use (\w+)', question, re.I)
        tool = m.group(1).lower() if m else 'search'
        arg = re.sub(r'.*use \w+\.?\s*', '', question, flags=re.I) or question
        print(f'Thought: I will use {tool} with {arg!r}')
        # Action
        result = TOOLS[tool](arg)
        # Observation
        print(f'Observation: {result}')
        context += result + ' '
        if 'no result' not in result:
            print(f'Answer: {result}')
            return result
    print('Step budget exhausted.')
    return None

react('What does MCP standardize? Use search.')
# Lesson: the loop is trivial; tool design + stop conditions are the engineering.

blocks.body: WITH clean AS (...) SELECT ... — named, testable steps. Recursive CTEs walk hierarchies (org charts, BOMs).
Know your row grain before you aggregate. Fan-out from a bad join multiplies rows silently — dedupe keys first, count(*) sanity-check after.
WHERE/JOIN/GROUP BY columns want indexes. Covering indexes avoid table lookups. But every index taxes writes — index for reads you actually run.
Extract (CDC or snapshot) → validate schema → transform (dbt) → load to warehouse → data-quality tests → publish marts. Idempotent reruns: same input, same output.
Kafka/Kinesis → stream processor (Flink/Spark Structured Streaming) → sink. Exactly-once = idempotent sinks + transactional offsets.
Airflow/Prefect: DAGs with retries, SLAs, and backfill. The scheduler is production — monitor it like production.
Row counts, null rates, freshness, distribution drift. A pipeline without tests is a rumor with compute costs.
Bronze (raw) → Silver (cleaned/conformed) → Gold (business marts). Never let analysts query Bronze directly.
Define the decision the model informs, then beat the dumb baseline (mean, majority class, heuristic) before any ML.
No feature may contain information unavailable at prediction time. Time-split validation, never random-split on time series.
Fraud: precision/recall tradeoff with dollar costs. Ranking: NDCG. Regression: MAE vs RMSE (outlier sensitivity). Never optimize accuracy on imbalanced data blindly.
Version data + code + model (registry). Shadow/canary deploy. Monitor prediction drift and label drift; retrain triggers, not schedules.
Chunk → embed → retrieve top-k → stuff into context → generate → cite. Evaluate retrieval (recall@k) separately from generation (faithfulness).
LoRA/QLoRA: train low-rank adapters, not full weights. Use for style/format/domain idioms — not for facts (facts go in retrieval).
ReAct loop: reason → act (tool) → observe → repeat. LangGraph for state machines; MCP for tool contracts. Stopping conditions and max-steps are safety features.
Quantization (GGUF/AWQ) trades precision for VRAM. Ollama/llama.cpp/vLLM serve open weights locally. Check the license (Llama, Apache-2.0, etc.) before commercial use.
Golden sets with rubrics; LLM-as-judge with human calibration; red-team prompts for injection/jailbreak. Evals are the spec.

answerBank.a: SQL — it's the lingua franca of data jobs and the relational model teaches set thinking. Then MongoDB for document shapes. The module sequences SQL fluency before documents.

answerBank.q: How do I break into data engineering?
answerBank.a: Pipeline fundamentals (orchestration, warehousing, quality) + one cloud data stack + a portfolio pipeline that runs on a schedule with tests. Certifications (AWS Data Engineer) help; the running pipeline proves.

answerBank.q: Do I need the math for ML?
answerBank.a: Yes for the deep end: linear algebra, probability, calculus — IL-02 gates it. For applied LLM engineering, less math and more systems thinking. The module marks which is which.
RAG for knowledge (grounding in your data, cheap to update); fine-tuning for behavior/format (tone, structure). Most production systems: RAG first, fine-tune only when RAG can't shape the behavior.

answerBank.q: Which open model should I self-host?
answerBank.a: Depends on your hardware and license needs — the module teaches the selection method (license card → quant ladder → benchmark your tasks), not a fixed answer, because the leaderboard changes monthly.
Raw ReAct first (learn the loop), then: linear tool use → LangChain; stateful/branching → LangGraph; data-grounded → LlamaIndex. The module's bake-off lab makes you defend the pick.

answerBank.q: How do I evaluate an LLM system honestly?
answerBank.a: Rubrics + human calibration: faithfulness (grounded in context?), relevance (answers the question?), plus task success. LLM-as-judge only with rubrics and spot-checked humans. Contamination checks on benchmarks.

glossary.definition: What one row represents (one order, one order-line). Every aggregation must respect the grain.
Row multiplication from one-to-many joins; silently inflates SUMs and COUNTs.
Common Table Expression (WITH clause): a named temporary result set; structures complex queries into testable steps.
Computation across a 'window' of related rows (ROW_NUMBER, RANK, LAG, running SUM) without collapsing rows.
Bronze (raw) → Silver (cleaned) → Gold (curated marts): progressive refinement zones in a lakehouse.
Re-runnable with identical results — the required property of pipeline tasks and backfills.
Change Data Capture: streaming row-level changes from a source database's log instead of full snapshots.
Data Build Tool: SQL-based transformation with tests, docs, and lineage — the T in ELT.
Freshness, completeness, validity, uniqueness, consistency — tested continuously, not assumed.
Training on information unavailable at prediction time; produces great validation scores and dead production models.
The dumb model (mean, majority class, heuristic) your ML must beat to justify its existence.
Prediction drift (input distribution shifts) or label drift (concept changes) degrading a deployed model.
Retrieval-Augmented Generation: retrieve relevant chunks, then generate grounded in them — with citations.
Dense vector representation of text/images; similarity search over embeddings powers retrieval.
Low-Rank Adaptation: fine-tune small adapter matrices (quantized base in QLoRA) instead of full weights.
Reason + Act loop: the agent reasons, calls a tool, observes the result, and repeats.
Model Context Protocol: a standard contract for exposing tools/data sources to AI models and agents.
Reducing model weight precision (FP16→INT8/INT4) to fit VRAM; the enabler of local open-weight serving.
Store indexed for embedding similarity search (pgvector, Pinecone, Qdrant, Weaviate).
Golden prompts + rubrics + automated judges measuring an LLM system's quality and safety over time.

faq.q: SQL or Python first for data work?
faq.a: SQL first — it's the lingua franca of data jobs and the interview filter. Python (pandas) follows for what SQL can't express cleanly. The course sequences them that way.

faq.q: Embed vs reference in MongoDB — is there a rule?
faq.a: Model for access patterns: embed what you read together and what's bounded; reference what's shared, unbounded, or updated independently. The module works both with real schemas.

faq.q: RAG or fine-tuning for my use case?
faq.a: RAG for facts that change or need citations; fine-tuning (LoRA) for style, format, and domain idioms. Most production systems use both — and evals decide the mix.

faq.q: Can I really self-host a useful model?
faq.a: Yes for many tasks: quantized 7–70B open-weight models on a decent GPU handle drafting, extraction, and classification. Frontier reasoning still favors API models — the module teaches the honest tradeoff.
Stanford's ML (229: supervised learning foundations) through reinforcement learning (234): the course's path from classical ML to RL and agents.

faq.q: How do I avoid leakage in practice?
faq.a: Time-split your validation, list every feature's 'as-of' timestamp, and ask 'would I know this at prediction time?' for each one. The ML module includes a leakage-audit checklist.

faq.q: Batch or streaming — how do I choose?
faq.a: Latency requirement decides: minutes-to-hours → batch (simpler, cheaper); seconds → streaming (harder, costlier). Most 'real-time' requests survive as micro-batch.

faq.q: How is this different from IL-26 (Data Analyst)?
faq.a: IL-07 is the engineering + ML depth track (pipelines, modeling, LLM systems). IL-26 is the analyst certification track (SQL/stats/BI/portfolio calibrated to hiring bars). Engineers build the pipes; analysts answer with them.

tips: Follow the guided path in order — each module unlocks the next. The sequence is the curriculum; skipping ahead breaks the chain.

This course maps to AWS Certified Data Engineer – Associate (DEA-C01) and AWS Certified Machine Learning Engineer – Associate (MLA-C01) (independent preparation — no affiliation). Weight your drill time toward the heaviest exam domains shown in the cert gates.
The math modules (Probability & Statistics, Linear Algebra Foundations) are load-bearing — finish them before the applied modules that assume them.
Quiz-gated modules need 70%+ to unlock the next. When you miss a question, ask Noah to walk you through the miss Socratically before re-attempting.
Do each hands-on lab twice — once following the guide, once from a blank screen. The second pass is where the skill sticks.
This is a 63-hour course: at 10 focused hours a week it takes about 2 months. Short daily sessions beat weekend cramming — pace it like a semester.
